title: Topical steroids and other creams for eczema
intro: Anti-inflammatory creams are the main medicine for treating flare-ups of atopic eczema. Topical corticosteroids work well, and when used correctly their risks are small. Non-steroid creams offer an alternative for sensitive areas or long-term control. Understanding how to use them reduces fear and improves results.

sections.heading: What topical steroids do
paragraphs: Corticosteroid creams and ointments reduce inflammation, redness and itching. They come in different strengths from mild to very potent. Doctors choose the strength according to the body area, age and severity. Mild strengths are used on the face and folds, and stronger ones on thick skin such as hands and feet.

sections.heading: How to use them
paragraphs: Apply a thin layer once or twice daily as prescribed to affected areas only, until the skin is clear or nearly so, usually for a few days to two weeks, then stop or reduce. Apply the steroid and moisturiser at different times, as directed. The fingertip unit measure, a line of cream from the fingertip to the first joint, covers an area about the size of two adult hands.

sections.heading: Side effects and concerns
paragraphs: With correct short-term use, side effects are uncommon. Prolonged use of strong steroids, particularly on thin skin like the face, can cause thinning, stretch marks, visible vessels and, rarely, absorption into the body. Many people fear steroids and undertreat, which leaves the eczema active. Follow the prescribed plan and ask questions.

sections.heading: Other options
paragraphs: Calcineurin inhibitor creams, such as tacrolimus and pimecrolimus, reduce inflammation without thinning skin and are used on sensitive areas such as face and eyelids or for long-term control, sometimes causing a temporary burning feeling at first. Other newer creams are available in some countries. Wet wrap therapy and antiseptic or antibiotic treatments are used for infected or severe eczema.

sections.heading: Preventing flares
paragraphs: Some people use anti-inflammatory creams on two days a week on previously affected areas to prevent flares, called proactive treatment, as advised by a doctor. Continue daily moisturising. See your doctor if eczema does not improve, if there are signs of infection or if you need creams frequently.

examples.title: Applying correctly
examples.text: Imagine your doctor prescribes a steroid cream for your child's elbows. You could apply a thin layer once daily until clear, and keep moisturising at other times.

examples.title: Addressing worries
examples.text: Suppose you are afraid of steroid side effects. You might share your concerns with your doctor and ask about strength, duration and how to stop safely.
